name: Ambulatory-Deep
geological_features: Slowly migrating storm systems that circle the planet
specific_features: Storm systems that follow predictable paths, appearing to walk around the planet
description: Ambulatory-Deep is a gas giant whose most distinctive feature is the behavior of its major storm systems: rather than remaining stationary or drifting chaotically, they follow predictable, repeating paths around the planet, migrating along the cloud bands in what atmospheric scientists have termed walking orbits. The largest of these ambulatory storms is twelve thousand kilometers across and completes a full circuit of the planet every ninety-seven standard days, its path as reliable as a train schedule.

The dense atmosphere is layered in muted blues and greys, less visually dramatic than many gas giants but possessed of an ordered beauty. The walking storms appear as darker knots against the cloud bands, their passage marked by turbulent wakes that take days to dissipate. From orbit, watching the storms process around the planet is hypnotic, their motion slow enough to be perceived but relentless. Deep in the atmosphere, convection cells drive the circulation that makes the walking possible.

Microbial life inhabits the temperate cloud layer, a zone of moderate pressure and temperature between the frozen upper atmosphere and the crushing depths below. These organisms are photosynthetic, utilizing the faint light that penetrates the upper cloud layers. They aggregate in vast sheets that drift with the cloud bands, their combined mass detectable as subtle density variations in atmospheric scans. The walking storms periodically disrupt these sheets, scattering them into new configurations.

Ambulatory-Deep's helium-3 reserves are substantial, and the predictability of its weather patterns makes it a more attractive harvesting target than most gas giants. The walking storms' paths can be mapped years in advance, allowing harvesting platforms to avoid them entirely. The microbial sheets in the temperate zone are thin enough that harvesting operations in the upper atmosphere are unlikely to disturb them significantly, though environmental reviews are ongoing.
